blocks.text: A 38-year-old man waiting for a scan sits with his knees bouncing, answers every question with one word, and then asks for the third time, "How long will it take?" He has not said he is frightened, yet almost everything he is doing tells you so. Noticing these signals, and responding to them kindly, is a clinical skill that can be learned.

blocks.markdown: Anxiety is very common among patients, because illness, unfamiliar surroundings, pain and uncertainty about the future are all threatening. Anxious patients may forget information, struggle to concentrate, or avoid examinations. Recognising anxiety early lets you adapt your approach, and the way you respond influences how much the patient trusts you and how well the consultation works.

blocks.title: Cues and concerns
blocks.text: A **cue** is a verbal or non-verbal hint that a patient has an emotional concern. A **concern** is the worry itself. Patients often give cues rather than stating concerns directly, so the clinician must notice and explore them.

blocks.caption: Common signs that a patient is anxious
rows: Saying "I'm worried" or "I'm nervous"; repeated questions; "what if" questions; asking about the worst case; rapid or pressured speech; long silences; changing the subject
Fidgeting, tapping, wringing hands, avoiding eye contact, rigid posture, tearfulness, looking at the door
Tremor, sweating, pallor, fast breathing, a fast pulse, a dry mouth
Delaying or declining an examination, arriving late or not at all

blocks.markdown: These signs are not specific. Tremor and fast breathing can come from fever, thyroid disease or lung disease, so **do not assume anxiety is the cause of physical signs**; use them as a prompt to ask, and make sure physical illness is not missed.

blocks.title: Picking up cues
blocks.prompt: A 29-year-old woman about to have a vaginal swab says, "I suppose it will be quick," glances at the door and clasps her hands tightly. Identify the cues and suggest a response.

steps.text: Verbal cue: the tentative remark "I suppose it will be quick" suggests she is hoping for something.
Non-verbal cues: glancing at the door and clasping her hands tightly suggest tension and a wish to escape.
Responding: name what you see gently, "You seem a little worried about this. Can you tell me what's on your mind?"
Listen to the answer and respond to the concern before continuing.

blocks.answer: Cues: tentative comment, glancing at door and clenched hands; response: a gentle open question that invites her to share the worry.

blocks.markdown:
### Responding with empathy

**Empathy** is understanding and acknowledging what the patient feels and showing that you have done so. A useful framework is **NURSE**:

- **N**ame the emotion: "It sounds like you're worried."
- **U**nderstand: "I can see why this feels frightening."
- **R**espect: "Many people would feel the same." or "You have coped well with a lot."
- **S**upport: "I'll be with you and we will go at your pace."
- **E**xplore: "Can you tell me more about what worries you most?"

Other helpful skills are **reflection** (repeating a key word back), **silence** (giving the patient time), and a calm voice and unhurried posture.

blocks.title: Avoid premature reassurance
blocks.text: Saying "Don't worry, it'll be fine" before you understand the worry can make the patient feel unheard and may be untrue. Explore first, then offer honest reassurance about what you do know.

blocks.caption: Empathic versus non-empathic responses
rows: "It's understandable to be scared. What worries you most?"
"It sounds like this is difficult for you. Can you tell me what's making it hard?"
"I'm sorry. That must make this very frightening."

blocks.title: Building an empathic reply
blocks.prompt: A 50-year-old man says, "My brother died after he had one of those operations." Write a reply using the NURSE steps.

steps.text: Name: "It sounds as though you are very worried about this operation."
Understand: "After losing your brother, I can see why this feels frightening."
Respect: "It takes courage to talk about this."
Support: "I will make sure the team hears your concerns, and I'll stay with you while we talk."
Explore: "Can you tell me what happened to your brother, and what worries you most for yourself?"

blocks.answer: An empathic reply that names the emotion, acknowledges the loss, respects the patient, offers support and explores the concern.

blocks.markdown:
### Adapting pace and vocabulary

Anxiety reduces how much people can take in. People also differ in education, language, hearing, health literacy and cultural background. To adapt:

1. **Find out what they already know** and what they want to know ("What have you been told so far?").
2. **Slow down**, use short sentences, and give **one idea at a time**.
3. **Use everyday words** and explain unavoidable terms.
4. **Check** understanding and give time for questions.
5. **Use aids** such as a drawing, a leaflet or an interpreter when needed, and make sure you are speaking to the patient and not only the interpreter.
6. **Repeat key points** and offer written information to take away.

items: Notice verbal and non-verbal cues before you start your task.
Name the emotion gently and ask an open question.
Avoid reassurance before you understand the worry.
Slow down and use plain language for an anxious patient.
Rule out physical causes of tremor, fast pulse or breathlessness.

blocks.title: Check the patient's level, not yours
blocks.text: The right pace and vocabulary depend on the patient. Ask what they already understand and let the answer set your starting point.

points: Anxiety shows through verbal cues, non-verbal behaviour and physical signs; none of these is specific, so explore rather than assume.
Respond with empathy: name the emotion, understand, respect, support and explore (NURSE).
Avoid premature reassurance, judgement and dismissal; explore the worry first.
Adapt your pace and vocabulary to the patient's level of understanding, using plain language, small chunks and checks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-verbal sign of anxiety?

options.text: Wringing hands and avoiding eye contact
Speaking in a calm, even voice
Leaning back with relaxed posture
Smiling and nodding at every question

questions.correctOptionText: Wringing hands and avoiding eye contact

distractorRationale.c: A relaxed posture is not a sign of anxiety.
distractorRationale.d: May be polite but is not a specific sign of anxiety.

questions.explanation: Fidgeting, hand wringing and avoiding eye contact are typical signs of tension. Because these signs are not specific, they should prompt exploration rather than a conclusion.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman waiting for results repeatedly asks "What if it's bad news?" and then says nothing for a while. How is this best described?

options.text: A verbal cue of anxiety that should be explored
A sign that she does not want the results
An indication that she is bored
A request to leave

questions.correctOptionText: A verbal cue of anxiety that should be explored

distractorRationale.a: Correct: repeated "what if" questions and silence are verbal cues of worry.
distractorRationale.c: Unlikely given the content of the question.

questions.explanation: Repeated worst-case questions and long silences suggest worry about the outcome. The best response is to acknowledge and explore the concern.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man says, "I am terrified they will find cancer." Which response is the most empathic and non-judgemental?

options.text: "That sounds really frightening. Can you tell me more about what worries you most?"
"There is no need to be terrified; it is almost certainly nothing."
"You shouldn't think like that."
"Let's just do the scan and see."

questions.correctOptionText: "That sounds really frightening. Can you tell me more about what worries you most?"

distractorRationale.a: Correct: names the emotion and invites him to explore.
distractorRationale.b: False reassurance that dismisses his fear.

questions.explanation: An empathic response acknowledges the emotion and invites the patient to say more. Premature reassurance or telling someone not to feel something closes the conversation.

questions.stem: A patient's hands are trembling and her pulse is 112 per minute. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Consider anxiety but also look for physical causes such as fever or thyroid disease
Assume anxiety and make no further checks
Tell her to calm down and re-measure later
Ignore the findings

questions.correctOptionText: Consider anxiety but also look for physical causes such as fever or thyroid disease
questions.explanation: A tremor and fast pulse can be caused by anxiety but also by many physical conditions. A clinician should avoid anchoring on anxiety and should look for other causes.

questions.stem: True or false: telling an anxious patient "Don't worry, it'll be fine" before asking about their concern is good practice.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Premature reassurance can make the patient feel unheard and may be untrue. It is better to explore the worry first and then offer honest reassurance.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with limited schooling is told he needs a lung function test. He looks confused and anxious as you describe "spirometry to assess airway obstruction". What should you do?

options.text: Slow down, use everyday words, and explain one step at a time while checking his understanding
Repeat the same sentence more loudly
Give him a technical leaflet and leave
Proceed without further explanation

questions.correctOptionText: Slow down, use everyday words, and explain one step at a time while checking his understanding

distractorRationale.c: A technical leaflet does not suit his level.

questions.explanation: Adapting means changing both pace and vocabulary. Short, plain explanations in single steps with checks suit a patient who is anxious and unfamiliar with medical terms.

questions.stem: Through an interpreter, a 40-year-old woman who speaks little English appears anxious. Which action best adapts your communication?

options.text: Speak directly to her, use short sentences, pause for interpretation and check understanding
Talk only to the interpreter
Speak much faster to save time
Ask her relative to decide for her

questions.correctOptionText: Speak directly to her, use short sentences, pause for interpretation and check understanding

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the patient remains the focus of the conversation.

questions.explanation: Even with an interpreter, you speak to the patient, use short phrases and check that the message was understood. This maintains rapport and reduces anxiety.

questions.stem: List verbal, non-verbal and physical signs that suggest a 35-year-old patient is anxious, and explain why you should not conclude that anxiety is the only cause of physical signs.
markingGuide: Verbal: expressing worry, repeated questions, what-if questions, pressured speech or silence
Non-verbal: fidgeting, hand wringing, avoiding eye contact, rigid posture, tearfulness
Physical: tremor, sweating, pallor, fast breathing or pulse
Signs are non-specific
Physical illness such as fever or thyroid disease can produce the same signs
Explore and assess rather than assume
questions.explanation: A good answer combines recognition with caution. Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion in the context of physical signs.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman about to undergo a procedure says, "I'm not sure I want to go through with this." Write a short empathic reply using the NURSE framework and explain why each step helps.
markingGuide: Name the emotion, for example worry or uncertainty
Understand: acknowledges why she may feel this way
Respect: normalises her feelings and respects her choice
Support: offers to go at her pace or stay with her
Explore: asks what worries her most
Avoids false reassurance and judgement
Explains that each step shows listening and builds trust
questions.explanation: The reply should be natural and not a recited list. Explaining why each step helps shows understanding of empathic communication.

questions.stem: Describe how you would adjust your pace and vocabulary when explaining a plan to an anxious 80-year-old patient who is hard of hearing and unfamiliar with medical terms.
markingGuide: Ask what the patient already knows and wants to know
Face the patient, speak clearly at a steady pace and reduce background noise
Short sentences and one idea at a time
Everyday words with explanation of any technical terms
Check understanding and invite questions
Use aids such as drawings or written information
Repeat key points
questions.explanation: Adaptation starts with finding the patient's level. Practical measures for hearing, language and anxiety all aim to reduce the load on the patient.
